parts.partTitle: How Requests Survive the Filter Chain

beats.headline: Why is your 403 error a black box?
beats.subline: Stop guessing and start tracing the DelegatingFilterProxy pipeline.
beats.narration: Many developers treat Spring Security like a black box, blindly disabling CSRF until tests pass. But underneath the DSL, it is just a standard Servlet filter pipeline.

beats.title: The Security Pipeline
beats.subtitle: From Servlet Container to Spring Beans

nodes.label: Servlet Container
nodes.detail: Tomcat or Jetty receives the raw HTTP request

nodes.label: DelegatingFilterProxy
nodes.detail: Standard Servlet filter that bridges to Spring context

nodes.label: FilterChainProxy
nodes.detail: The central engine managing multiple security chains

nodes.label: SecurityFilterChain
nodes.detail: Ordered list of filters (CSRF, Auth, Exception)

beats.narration: Tomcat knows nothing about Spring beans. DelegatingFilterProxy bridges that gap, handing off to FilterChainProxy, which routes your request through the correct ordered security chain.

beats.title: Defining Multiple Chains

steps.explanation: Crucial! Without this, the first chain swallows all requests, breaking your fallback chains.
Determines evaluation priority. Lower numbers are checked first by the FilterChainProxy.

beats.narration: Use securityMatcher to isolate your API from your web portal. Without it, the first chain matches everything, and your fallback rules will never be reached.

beats.title: AuthN vs AuthZ
beats.narration: Conflating these two is the root of most security bugs. AuthN asks who you are, producing 401s. AuthZ asks if you have permission, producing 403s.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Password hashing and the DelegatingPasswordEncoder →
beats.narration: That is the high-level architecture. In Part 2, we look at how to store passwords securely and why you should never use MD5 or SHA-256.

beats.headline: Is your password hash actually safe?
beats.subline: MD5 and SHA-256 are fast, and that makes them dangerous.
beats.narration: If you are using MD5 or SHA-256 to hash passwords, you are inviting disaster. These algorithms are too fast, making them trivial to crack with modern GPUs.

beats.title: Adaptive Hashing
beats.narration: Use BCrypt for standard workloads. If you need maximum resistance against ASIC-based cracking, use Argon2id—it is memory-hard, making it significantly more expensive to brute-force.

beats.title: Future-Proofing Hashes

steps.explanation: Prepends {id} to hashes, allowing you to migrate algorithms without forcing users to reset passwords.

beats.narration: Never hardcode one encoder. Use DelegatingPasswordEncoder. It prefixes your hashes with the algorithm ID, letting you seamlessly upgrade from BCrypt to Argon2id as your security needs evolve.

beats.title: UserDetailsService Flow
beats.subtitle: How DaoAuthenticationProvider works

nodes.label: PasswordEncoder
nodes.detail: Checks raw password vs stored hash

beats.narration: UserDetailsService only fetches the data. The DaoAuthenticationProvider handles the heavy lifting, verifying the password and clearing credentials from memory to keep your heap clean.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.narration: Your passwords are now safe. In Part 3, we tackle the most common API vulnerability: IDOR, and how to stop it with method-level security.

beats.headline: URL security cannot stop IDOR.
beats.subline: A valid user can still access another user's private data.
beats.narration: URL rules only check the route, not the resource owner. If you rely only on URL security, an attacker can simply change an ID in the path to steal data.

beats.title: Method-Level Authorization

steps.explanation: Executes logic before the method runs. If it returns false, Spring throws AccessDeniedException.
Spring Expression Language calls your custom bean to verify ownership dynamically.

beats.narration: Use @PreAuthorize to delegate ownership checks to a dedicated bean. This ensures that even if you change your controller, the security logic remains tightly coupled to the data access.

beats.title: Custom Security Evaluator

steps.explanation: Centralize your business rules here. This is the only place you need to audit for IDOR bugs.

beats.narration: This evaluator handles both role checks and ownership logic. By centralizing this, you eliminate the risk of inconsistent security checks across your entire service layer.

beats.title: The Proxy Trap

top.label: Internal Call

bottom.label: Bean Boundary

beats.narration: Watch out for internal calls. If you call an @PreAuthorize method from within the same class, you bypass the proxy. Always move privileged logic to a separate bean.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: URL security is not enough for IDOR
Avoid internal calls to bypass proxies
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Async threads and CSRF protection →
beats.narration: You are now building secure APIs. In Part 4, we finish by solving the ThreadLocal context propagation issue and when to actually disable CSRF.

beats.headline: Why does your security context disappear in async threads?
beats.subline: ThreadLocal is the culprit, but there is a clean fix.
beats.narration: When you hand work off to an @Async thread, your security context vanishes. That is because ThreadLocal is local to the thread, not the request.

beats.title: Propagating Security Context

steps.explanation: Automatically copies the SecurityContext from the parent thread to the background worker thread.

beats.narration: Wrap your executor in DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor. It copies the security context onto the worker thread, ensuring your @PreAuthorize checks work even in background tasks.

beats.title: CSRF: To Disable or Not?
beats.narration: Only disable CSRF if your API is stateless and uses Bearer tokens. If you use cookies, you are vulnerable to cross-site forgery and must keep CSRF enabled.

beats.title: CSRF Attack Vector
beats.subtitle: Why browsers are the danger
beats.narration: Browsers attach cookies automatically. A malicious site can trigger a request to your app, and if you don't check for a CSRF token, the bank app thinks the user intended it.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
takeaways: Disable CSRF only for stateless APIs
